claim: The E. coli 70S ribosome is a large (2.4 MDa) ribonucleoprotein consisting of a small (30S) and large (50S) subunit.
source: In Escherichia coli (E. coli), the 70S ribosome is a large (2.4 MDa) ribonucleoprotein consisting of a small (30S) and large (50S) subunit.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosome structure and composition.

claim: The 30S subunit can be reconstituted in vitro from 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and 20 ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) in a high temperature, high Mg2+ environment.
source: Remarkably, the 30S subunit can be reconstituted in vitro from 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and 20 ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) in a high temperature, high Mg2+ environment (Traub and Nomura, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Traub and Nomura, 1969.

claim: Early work by Nomura and colleagues established the order and dependencies of r-protein binding in the assembling 30S subunit under equilibrium conditions.
source: Early work by Nomura and colleagues established the order and dependencies of r-protein binding in the assembling 30S subunit under equilibrium conditions (Figure 1A) (Mizushima and Nomura, 1970; Held et al., 1973, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mizushima and Nomura, 1970; Held et al., 1973, 1974.

claim: Primary r-proteins bind directly to the 5′-, central and 3′-domains of 16S rRNA in the early stages of assembly.
source: In the early stages of assembly, primary r-proteins bind directly to the 5′-, central and 3′-domains of 16S rRNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Held et al., 1973; Stern et al., 1989 in the context of the sentence.

claim: Initial r-protein binding events lead to changes in the rRNA structure and facilitate subsequent binding of secondary and tertiary r-proteins.
source: These initial r-protein binding events lead to changes in the rRNA structure, and facilitate subsequent binding of secondary and tertiary r-proteins (Held et al., 1973; Stern et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Held et al., 1973; Stern et al., 1989.

claim: Assembly can proceed through multiple parallel pathways even in the presence of r-protein binding dependencies.
source: These studies have revealed that even in the presence of r-protein binding dependencies, assembly can proceed through multiple parallel pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple studies mentioned in the preceding sentence including Adilakshmi et al., 2008; Ridgeway et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2014; Talkington et al., 2005; Bunner et al., 2010a; Mulder et al., 2010.

claim: Misfolded rRNA structure leads to stable kinetic traps during in vitro 30S reconstitution, inhibiting the binding of several secondary and tertiary r-proteins.
source: In addition, a large body of evidence indicates that misfolded rRNA structure leads to stable kinetic traps during in vitro 30S reconstitution, inhibiting the binding of several secondary and tertiary r-proteins and limiting the efficiency of the reconstitution (Reviewed in Sykes and Williamson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review by Sykes and Williamson, 2009.

claim: In the cell, 30S assembly is fast and efficient, proceeding with the help of numerous assembly factors.
source: In the cell, 30S assembly is fast and efficient, proceeding with the help of numerous assembly factors, including enzymes that directly modify the 16S rRNA and r-proteins, as well as a number of RNA-binding chaperones and GTPases that assist in RNA folding (Reviewed in Wilson and Nierhaus, 2007; Shajani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews by Wilson and Nierhaus, 2007; Shajani et al., 2011.

claim: Some assembly factors, such as RimM and RbfA, may promote efficient assembly by binding co-transcriptionally to the nascent rRNA to facilitate folding and to prevent the formation of kinetic traps.
source: Previous studies suggest that some assembly factors, such as RimM and RbfA, may promote efficient assembly by binding co-transcriptionally to the nascent rRNA to facilitate folding and to prevent the formation of kinetic traps (Williamson, 2003; Clatterbuck Soper et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williamson, 2003; Clatterbuck Soper et al., 2013.

claim: Several assembly factors, including RbfA, Era, RsgA, and KsgA, bind immature subunits and block them from prematurely entering the translation cycle.
source: Cryo-EM reconstructions indicate that several assembly factors, including RbfA (Datta et al., 2007; Jomaa et al., 2011b), the GTPases Era (Sharma et al., 2005) and RsgA (Guo et al., 2011), and the 16S rRNA methyltransferase KsgA (Boehringer et al., 2012), bind immature subunits and block them from prematurely entering the translation cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Datta et al., 2007; Jomaa et al., 2011b; Sharma et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2011; Boehringer et al., 2012.

claim: RimP has been implicated in 30S assembly but has no known connection to the overall assembly factor network.
source: Other factors, such as RimP, have been implicated in 30S assembly but have no known connection to the overall assembly factor network (Nord et al., 2009; Bunner et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nord et al., 2009; Bunner et al., 2010b.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry provides a high-throughput method for precisely measuring the relative levels of proteins in a complex mixture.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry (qMS) provides a high-throughput method for precisely measuring the relative levels of proteins in a complex mixture (Charollais et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Charollais et al., 2003.

claim: qMS has been used to determine the composition of r-proteins within ribosomal assembly intermediates isolated from cells, revealing the binding dependencies of late-associating r-proteins.
source: Recently, qMS has been used to determine the composition of r-proteins within ribosomal assembly intermediates isolated from cells, revealing the binding dependencies of late-associating r-proteins on earlier binding r-proteins and assembly factors (Chen and Williamson, 2013; Clatterbuck Soper et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Leong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Williamson, 2013; Clatterbuck Soper et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Leong et al., 2013.

claim: Automated data collection and downstream image processing has greatly improved the throughput of single-particle EM analysis.
source: Automated data collection and downstream image processing has greatly improved the throughput of single-particle EM analysis, facilitating the rapid analysis of even highly heterogeneous samples in a short period of time (Suloway et al., 2005; Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Suloway et al., 2005; Lander et al., 2009.

claim: Automated random conical tilt (RCT) data collection enables three-dimensional reconstructions of each subpopulation identified in a sample.
source: In addition, automated random conical tilt (RCT) data collection enables three-dimensional reconstructions of each subpopulation identified in a sample (Radermacher et al., 1987; Yoshioka et al., 2007; Voss et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Radermacher et al., 1987; Yoshioka et al., 2007; Voss et al., 2010.

claim: Five distinct groups of 30S assembly intermediates were observed in WT E. coli, distinguished by their conformation and r-protein content.
source: Our analysis of sucrose gradient fractions from the E. coli 30S peak revealed five distinct groups of assembly intermediates distinguished by their conformation and r-protein content (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D showing qMS and EM analysis.

claim: Group I particles comprised the earliest observed assembly intermediates with the body and platform domains intact but no head domain density.
source: Group I particles comprised the earliest observed assembly intermediates with the body and platform domains intact but no head domain density (Figure 1D, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2A.

claim: In Group II particles, the head appears to be completely unanchored from the platform domain.
source: In Group II, the head appears to be completely unanchored from the platform domain, swinging well away from the helix 23/S11 interaction region (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Group III, the head appears to be docked along the platform domain but angled away from its final resting spot along the body domain.
source: In contrast, in Group III the head appears to be docked along the platform domain as it is in mature subunits, but angled away from its final resting spot along the body domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RCT volumes for classes from both Groups II and III suggest that late-binding proteins S2 and S3 may be missing from these particles.
source: RCT volumes for classes from both Groups suggest that late-binding proteins S2 and S3 may be missing from these particles, consistent with the relatively low levels of the proteins observed by qMS (Figure 1C, Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data in Figure 2B,C and qMS data in Figure 1C.

claim: Groups IV and V represent very late assembly intermediates and mature subunits.
source: Classes belonging to Groups IV and V represent very late assembly intermediates and mature subunits, as observed by 2D class averages and 3D RCT reconstructions (Figure 1D, Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2D-H.

claim: RCT reconstructions of Group IV classes appear to lack some density in the platform region, suggesting that these particles may primarily be late intermediates depleted of very late-binders such as S21 and S2.
source: RCT reconstructions of Group IV classes appear to lack some density in the platform region, suggesting that these particles may primarily be late intermediates depleted of very late-binders such as S21 and S2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 2D and inference from the observed density.

claim: The central pseudoknot (PK) that connects the 5′-body domain of the 16S rRNA with the 3′-head domain appears to be formed in Group III but unformed in Group II particles.
source: In particular, the central PK, the long-range tertiary interaction within 16S rRNA that anchors the head domain to the body and platform, appears to be formed in Group III but unformed in Group II particles.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences observed between Group II and Group III particles in EM data.

claim: The detachment of the head from the platform in Group II classes suggests that these particles may have unstable or unformed central PK regions.
source: The detachment of the head from the platform in Group II classes suggests that these particles may have unstable or unformed central PK regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of head detachment in Group II particles.

claim: Deletion of RimP has a much stronger effect on central PK exposure than either RimM or RbfA.
source: Surprisingly, we found that deletion of RimP has a much stronger effect on central PK exposure than either RimM or RbfA, suggesting that RimP may have a more direct role in central PK formation (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNase H assay data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Group II particles are most abundant in ΔrimP and BW-25113+pU23.
source: Group II particles were most abundant in ΔrimP and BW-25113+pU23 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The levels of particles belonging to Group II in each strain was consistent with the amount of cleavage observed for anti-PK-oligo-dependent RNase H cleavage.
source: overall the levels of particles belonging to Group II in each strain was consistent with the amount of cleavage observed for anti-PK-oligo-dependent RNase H cleavage (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNase H assay data and EM data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The ΔrimP strain shows an increase in 30S and 50S particles with a concomitant decrease in 70S particles, compared to the WT strain.
source: In agreement with previous studies, the ΔrimP strain shows an increase in 30S and 50S particles with a concomitant decrease in 70S particles, compared to the WT strain (Figure 4A) (Nord et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Nord et al., 2009.

claim: S3 and S21 are significantly depleted relative to other r-proteins in both WT and ΔrimP strains, across all fractions.
source: Hierarchal clustering of r-protein abundances normalized to that of S4, reveals significant depletion of S3 and S21 relative to other r-proteins in both strains, across all fractions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qMS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: S2 and S12 are more depleted in the ΔrimP strain relative to the WT strain.
source: Furthermore, S2 and S12 are more depleted in the ΔrimP strain relative to the WT strain.
evidence: This is observed in the qMS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The 30S particles in the early fractions of both WT and ΔrimP strains have higher fraction labeled values than the 70S ribosomes, indicating that the early fractions contain significant amounts of 30S assembly intermediates.
source: The qMS analysis of the fractions containing 30S particles and 70S ribosomes from the WT and ΔrimP strains reveals that the 30S particles in the early fractions of both strains have higher fL values than the 70S ribosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). This indicates that the early fractions of both strains contain significant amounts of 30S assembly intermediates, and that these intermediates are competent to mature into 70S ribosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-labeling qMS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a delay in 30S assembly in the ΔrimP strain compared to the WT strain, corresponding to an accumulation of assembly intermediates.
source: This indicates that there is a delay in 30S assembly in the ΔrimP strain compared to the WT strain, corresponding to an accumulation of assembly intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from the pulse-labeling data showing differences in fraction labeled values between WT and ΔrimP.

claim: In the ΔrimP strain, the most depleted r-proteins in the 30S intermediates are those with the highest fraction labeled values in the 70S ribosomes, and these correspond to the latest binding r-proteins.
source: Moreover, the data show that in the ΔrimP strain, the most depleted r-proteins in the 30S intermediates are those with the highest fraction labeled values in the 70S ribosomes, and these correspond to the latest binding r-proteins.
evidence: This is observed in the pulse-labeling data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Primary binding r-proteins such as S4 that are highly abundant in assembly intermediates in the ΔrimP strain have large values of precursor pool size (P).
source: The data show that primary binding r-proteins such as S4 that are highly abundant in assembly intermediates in the ΔrimP strain have large values of P (p = 0.12 or 12%), confirming that the assembly intermediates are on-pathway (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-labeling kinetics data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Depleted r-proteins such as S12 have small precursor pools (P ∼ 0) in the ΔrimP strain.
source: In contrast, depleted r-proteins such as S12 have small precursor pools (P ∼ 0) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-labeling kinetics data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: There is a marked delay in S12 binding in the ΔrimP strain relative to WT.
source: This indicates a marked delay in S12 binding in the ΔrimP strain relative to WT.
evidence: This is inferred from the precursor pool size data showing S12 clustering with late binders despite being an early binder in WT.

claim: The intermediate assembly species in ΔrimP are on-pathway.
source: Together, these pulse-labeling data show that the intermediate assembly species are on-pathway and that incorporation of S12 and late-binding proteins S2, S21 and S3 is delayed during 30S assembly in the absence of RimP.
evidence: This is supported by the pulse-labeling kinetics data showing that intermediates eventually mature into 70S ribosomes.

claim: Incorporation of S12 and late-binding proteins S2, S21 and S3 is delayed during 30S assembly in the absence of RimP.
source: Together, these pulse-labeling data show that the intermediate assembly species are on-pathway and that incorporation of S12 and late-binding proteins S2, S21 and S3 is delayed during 30S assembly in the absence of RimP.
evidence: This is supported by the pulse-labeling kinetics data and precursor pool size analysis.

claim: There is a dramatic increase in the abundance of Group II intermediates in ΔrimP relative to WT.
source: However, the relative number of particles within each Group differs significantly between the two strains, with a dramatic increase in the abundance of Group II intermediates in ΔrimP relative to WT (Figure 1D, Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 5B comparing WT and ΔrimP.

claim: Group II intermediates are enriched by >3-fold in ΔrimP samples when directly compared to WT.
source: In particular, Group II is enriched by >3-fold in ΔrimP samples when directly compared to WT (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 5C directly comparing WT and ΔrimP.

claim: The location of the head volume is highly variable in Group II particles in both 2D class averages and 3D RCT volumes.
source: In both 2D class averages and 3D RCT volumes, the location of the head volume is highly variable (residues 912–920) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The regions of high variance in Group II particles are mainly localized to the head domain.
source: The regions of high variance are mainly localized to the head domain, which can sample a substantial range of motion, from locations close to the S11-binding region in the platform domain to the S4-binding region of the body domain.
evidence: This is supported by variance analysis of RCT volumes shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Head movement in Group II particles is constrained by a short but highly flexible linker, likely comprising the 3′-end of helix 27 and the 3′-strand of the unformed h2 (16S residues 910–919).
source: Analysis of Group II particles in 2D by Maskiton (Yoshioka et al., 2013) recapitulates this result and additionally indicates that head movement is constrained by a short but highly flexible linker (Video 2), likely comprising the 3′-end of helix 27 and the 3′-strand of the unformed h2 (16S residues 910–919).
evidence: This claim is supported by Maskiton analysis shown in Video 2 and structural inference.

claim: Group II particles may contain a nearly complete complement of r-proteins in the head domain.
source: The similarity in size suggests that Group II particles may contain a nearly complete complement of r-proteins in the head domain, and that head domain assembly can occur prior to central PK formation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of RCT volumes with filtered PDB models.

claim: Head domain assembly can occur prior to central PK formation.
source: The similarity in size suggests that Group II particles may contain a nearly complete complement of r-proteins in the head domain, and that head domain assembly can occur prior to central PK formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Group II particles with assembled head domains but unformed central PK.

claim: Affinity purified ΔrimP intermediates show very depleted S2 and S12, with partial depletion of S3 and S5.
source: The relative abundance of each r-protein, normalized with respect to S4, shows that S2 and S12 are very depleted in 30S particles with PK instability, with partial depletion of S3 and S5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qMS data of affinity purified intermediates shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The affinity purified particles show a high abundance of most of the 3′-domain r-proteins relative to early 5′-domain binder, S4.
source: Furthermore, the affinity purified particles show a high abundance of most of the 3′-domain r-proteins relative to early 5′-domain binder, S4.
evidence: This is observed in the qMS data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: With the exception of S2 and S3, the uniform abundance of all the 3′-domain r-proteins in the purified intermediates suggests that head domain formation is not perturbed until the very late stages of assembly.
source: With the exception of S2 and S3, the uniform abundance of all the 3′-domain r-proteins in the purified intermediates suggests that head domain formation is not perturbed until the very late stages of assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the qMS data showing uniform abundance of most 3′-domain proteins.

claim: Group I cryo-EM structures lack density for the entire 3′-domain, including all RNA and r-proteins comprising the head domain and helices 44 and 45 of the 3′-minor domain.
source: As expected, the Group I structures lack density for the entire 3′-domain, including all RNA and r-proteins comprising the head domain and helices 44 and 45 of the 3′-minor domain (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 16S rRNA helix 27 lies completely outside the density in all Group I reconstructions, indicating that this final secondary structural element of the central domain is not present in these particles.
source: In addition, 16S rRNA helix 27 lies completely outside the density in all Group I reconstructions, indicating that this final secondary structural element of the central domain is not present in these particles.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM reconstructions shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The Group I reconstructions clearly lack density for both S5 and S12.
source: Notably, the Group I reconstructions also clearly lack density for both S5 and S12, consistent with their observed depletion by qMS.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM reconstructions shown in Figure 6B and is consistent with qMS data.

claim: S5 may be present in Group II particles, while S12 is likely missing from both Group I and Group II intermediates.
source: The relatively high levels of S5 in comparison to S12 suggest that S5 may be present in Group II particles, while S12 is likely missing from both intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from the qMS data showing different depletion levels for S5 and S12.

claim: Variability between Group I structures mainly arises from differences in the platform region.
source: In agreement with variations observed by 3D classification of the particles, this codimensional PCA revealed that variability between these structures mainly arises from differences in the platform region (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by codimensional PCA analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Structural stability within the platform region may be dependent on assembly and docking of the 3′-domain.
source: Together, these analyses of Group I cryo-EM particles suggest that structural stability within the platform region may be dependent on assembly and docking of the 3′-domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed variability in the platform region of Group I particles which lack the 3′-domain.

claim: The central pseudoknot is essential for translation.
source: The central PK is essential for translation (Brink et al., 1993; Poot et al., 1998) and is conserved in all kingdoms of life.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brink et al., 1993; Poot et al., 1998.

claim: The central pseudoknot is conserved in all kingdoms of life.
source: The central PK is essential for translation (Brink et al., 1993; Poot et al., 1998) and is conserved in all kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosome structure.

claim: The essential ribosomal biogenesis factor Mrd1 was implicated in central PK formation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Recently, the essential ribosomal biogenesis factor Mrd1 was implicated in central PK formation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Segerstolpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Segerstolpe et al., 2013.

claim: Mrd1 contains multiple RNA-binding domains (RBDs) and binds directly to 18S rRNA helices h27 and h28.
source: Mrd1 contains multiple RNA-binding domains (RBDs) and binds directly to 18S rRNA helices h27 and h28, two secondary structural elements that reside in close proximity to the central PK in the mature small subunit structure (Segerstolpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Segerstolpe et al., 2013.

claim: RimP is composed of two RBDs.
source: Similarly, RimP is composed of two RBDs, and may play an analogous role in binding to 16S rRNA regions adjacent to the central PK.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RimP structure.

claim: RimP may play an analogous role to Mrd1 in binding to 16S rRNA regions adjacent to the central PK.
source: Similarly, RimP is composed of two RBDs, and may play an analogous role in binding to 16S rRNA regions adjacent to the central PK.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural similarity between RimP and Mrd1.

claim: RimP acts during the early and late stages of 30S subunit biogenesis to assist in the stabilization of the central pseudoknot.
source: We propose that RimP acts during the early and late stages of 30S subunit biogenesis to assist in the stabilization of the central pseudoknot, allowing for the subsequent incorporation of central-PK binding r-proteins S5 and S12 and late binding r-proteins S2, S3 and S21 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study, shown in Figure 7.

claim: RimP stabilization of the central pseudoknot allows for the subsequent incorporation of central-PK binding r-proteins S5 and S12 and late binding r-proteins S2, S3 and S21.
source: We propose that RimP acts during the early and late stages of 30S subunit biogenesis to assist in the stabilization of the central pseudoknot, allowing for the subsequent incorporation of central-PK binding r-proteins S5 and S12 and late binding r-proteins S2, S3 and S21 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing depletion of these proteins in ΔrimP.

claim: During the early stages of 30S biogenesis, premature central PK formation is blocked by a structure within the 16S 5′-leader that is mutually exclusive with h1.
source: During the early stages of 30S biogenesis, premature central PK formation is blocked by a structure within the 16S 5′-leader that is mutually exclusive with h1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about 30S assembly.

claim: RbfA is thought to bind to the leader sequence and promote formation of h1 during the late stages of assembly.
source: RbfA is thought to bind to the leader sequence and promote formation of h1 during the late stages of assembly, and may act synergistically with RimP to stabilize the central PK.
evidence: This is based on previous knowledge about RbfA function.

claim: RbfA may act synergistically with RimP to stabilize the central PK.
source: RbfA is thought to bind to the leader sequence and promote formation of h1 during the late stages of assembly, and may act synergistically with RimP to stabilize the central PK.
evidence: This is speculated based on the roles of both factors in central PK formation.

claim: RimM may act independently of RimP to facilitate assembly of the head domain regardless of the status of central PK formation.
source: In contrast, RimM may act independently of RimP to facilitate assembly of the head domain regardless of the status of central PK formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ΔrimM predominantly contains Group III intermediates with anchored heads, while ΔrimP contains Group II intermediates with unanchored heads.

claim: RimP might be one of the earliest factors to act upon the assembling 30S subunit.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that RimP might be one of the earliest factors to act upon the assembling 30S subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RimP affects early intermediates and central PK formation.

claim: RimP has previously been shown to accelerate binding of S5 and S12 by twofold and sixfold, respectively, in in vitro reconstitution assays.
source: Interestingly, RimP has previously been shown to accelerate binding of S5 and S12 by twofold and sixfold, respectively, in in vitro reconstitution assays (Bunner et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bunner et al., 2010b.

claim: Addition of RimP to 30S reconstitution experiments may help to promote central PK formation and avoid the kinetically unfavorable Group I and Group II intermediates.
source: Together with our findings, these previous results suggest that addition of RimP to 30S reconstitution experiments may help to promote central PK formation and avoid the kinetically unfavorable Group I and Group II intermediates.
evidence: This is speculated based on the role of RimP in central PK formation observed in this study.

claim: Group I-like class averages were highly abundant at early time-points during in vitro 30S reconstitution.
source: In previous EM studies of assembly intermediates present during in vitro 30S reconstitution, Group I-like class averages were highly abundant at early time-points during assembly (Mulder et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mulder et al., 2010.

claim: Group II-like classes are present during the early stages of in vitro 30S assembly.
source: Intriguingly, Group II-like classes are also present during the early stages of assembly, although they were uncharacterized in that study (See Figure 1B in Mulder et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mulder et al., 2010.

claim: The presence of Group I and II-like classes subsides with the incorporation of S5 and S12 during in vitro reconstitution.
source: The presence of Group I and II-like classes subsides with the incorporation of S5 and S12, as measured by pulse-chase followed by qMS.
evidence: This is inferred from previous in vitro studies.

claim: Kinetically unfavorable pre-central PK conformations remain viable on-pathway intermediates.
source: These previous in vitro results agree with the present in vivo observations that kinetically unfavorable pre-central PK conformations remain viable on-pathway intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: RimP has previously been shown to bind to free 30S subunits resolved on sucrose gradients, but not complete 70S ribosomes.
source: RimP has previously been shown to bind to free 30S subunits resolved on sucrose gradients, but not complete 70S ribosomes, indicating that it directly interacts with 30S assembly intermediates (Nord et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nord et al., 2009.

claim: RimP directly interacts with 30S assembly intermediates.
source: RimP has previously been shown to bind to free 30S subunits resolved on sucrose gradients, but not complete 70S ribosomes, indicating that it directly interacts with 30S assembly intermediates (Nord et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RimP binds to 30S but not 70S particles.

claim: The combined EM/qMS approach should have immediate and broad applicability to study of the role of other ribosome assembly factors as well as macromolecular assembly processes involving other bacterial and eukaryotic cellular machines.
source: The combined EM/qMS approach employed here should have immediate and broad applicability to study of the role of other ribosome assembly factors as well as macromolecular assembly processes involving other bacterial and eukaryotic cellular machines.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader applicability of the method developed in this study.
